analysis.one_liner: Removes the exemption that lets oil and gas drilling waste be dumped without hazardous-waste rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to regulate oil and gas drilling waste as hazardous waste was referred to a House committee and its subcommittee in July 2023 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1988, waste from drilling for oil and gas — drilling fluids and the salty, chemical-laden water that comes up with the oil — has been exempt from the nation's hazardous-waste disposal rules. This bill would end that exemption. Within a year, the EPA would have to test whether drilling waste meets the hazardous-waste criteria, write disposal rules for the parts that are hazardous, and tighten rules for landfills that take the rest, including groundwater monitoring and cleanup requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near drilling waste disposal sites — landfills, injection pits, and spreading operations — especially in drilling-heavy states like Pennsylvania. The bill's named goal is protecting human health and the environment from waste that can contain heavy metals, salts, and naturally occurring radioactive material. Stricter disposal rules, groundwater monitoring, and financial assurance requirements would lower the chance of contaminated drinking water and polluted land near these sites.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the regulatory exemption for drilling fluids, produced waters, and other oil, gas, and geothermal exploration and production waste under the Solid Waste Disposal Act (the law behind hazardous-waste regulation), so that waste would be regulated like other industrial waste [S2][S3].

Within one year, the EPA would have to determine whether this waste meets the hazardous-waste criteria, list as hazardous whatever qualifies, and write handling and disposal regulations for it, with flexibility to adapt the rules to the waste's special characteristics as long as they protect health and the environment [S2][S3].

For waste that is not hazardous, the EPA would have to tighten the rules for landfills and other facilities that accept it, at minimum requiring groundwater monitoring to detect contamination, siting criteria for facilities, and corrective action and financial assurance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would face new testing, handling, and disposal costs for waste they currently dispose of under weaker rules. Geothermal energy producers would face the same requirements. Disposal costs could rise for companies and potentially flow through to energy prices, and landfill operators handling this waste would face monitoring and financial assurance requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers, geothermal producers

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the EPA to complete a hazard determination, list qualifying wastes, and write two sets of regulations within a single year of enactment — an unusually short deadline for a rulemaking of this scale, and one an agency could plausibly miss [S3].

Regulating produced water as hazardous could sharply raise disposal costs for drillers, and those costs could add to energy prices or push waste handling toward cheaper, less-regulated channels if the rules are not written carefully; industry has long argued the waste is more like ordinary industrial byproduct than hazardous waste (a general-policy objection, not drawn from the provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: closing a nearly four-decade-old loophole so the same disposal rules that apply to other industrial waste also apply to oil and gas drilling waste, with groundwater monitoring as the backstop for anything not classified as hazardous. The costs are real but ordinary ones — disposal compliance costs for producers — and the bill gives the EPA flexibility to tailor requirements to the waste's characteristics. The one-year deadline is tight. On balance the public-health protections outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee from July 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025 — no markup, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 20, 2023 by Rep. Matt Cartwright with 29 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].

The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No further action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers keep disposing of drilling waste under the current exemption, avoiding the testing, handling, and disposal costs this bill would have imposed. People living near disposal sites remain without the groundwater monitoring and financial assurance rules the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers keeping the waste exemption

sides.party_line_note: All 30 initial supporters — the sponsor and 29 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors appear in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill's whole purpose is to end the industry's exemption from hazardous-waste disposal rules, subjecting drilling fluids and produced water to testing, handling, and disposal requirements and new costs. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against the residents who live near disposal sites.
The bill treats geothermal exploration and production waste the same as oil and gas waste, so geothermal operators would face the same new disposal rules and costs.

Landfills and facilities accepting this waste would face groundwater monitoring, siting criteria, corrective action, and financial assurance requirements, but could also gain business if hazardous classification pushes waste to permitted facilities. The stricter rules serve the surrounding communities' interest.
